subject: chemistry
title: Weak acids and Ka
key_idea: A weak acid is only partly dissociated, and the extent is measured by Ka. For a weak acid, [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]) when two approximations hold. pKa = −log₁₀Ka, so a larger Ka means a smaller pKa.

blocks.text: Acids differ in how far they dissociate in water. This section covers the difference and what it does to pH.

items.meaning: An acid that dissociates completely in water.
An acid that dissociates only slightly in water, so an equilibrium is set up.
The fraction of acid molecules that have donated H⁺.

items: Weak bases, such as NH₃, also dissociate only slightly in water.
A strong and a weak acid of the same concentration have different pH, because their [H⁺] differ.
Neither is the same as **concentrated** or **dilute**. Those words describe how much acid is dissolved, not how far it dissociates.
Strong acids dissociate completely. Weak acids dissociate partly.
Equimolar weak acids have a higher pH than strong acids.

blocks.text: Ka is the equilibrium constant for a weak acid dissociating. pKa puts it on a log scale like pH.

items: A larger Ka means a stronger weak acid, with more dissociation.
A smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Ethanoic acid has Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³ and pKa = 4.76.
To reverse it, Ka = 10^(−pKa).
Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA] for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻.
pKa = −log₁₀Ka. Larger Ka means smaller pKa.

sections.heading: The pH of a weak acid

blocks.text: The exact equilibrium needs a quadratic equation, so two approximations are made. This section sets out the method.

items: [HA] at equilibrium ≈ [HA] before dissociation. This holds because only a very small fraction dissociates, so [HA] ≫ [H⁺].
[H⁺] = [A⁻] at equilibrium. This holds because H⁺ from the dissociation of water is negligible.

diagram.alt: A practice question finding the hydrogen ion concentration of a weak acid.
diagram.question: A weak acid HA has Ka = {k} × 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³. Its concentration is {c} mol/dm³. Calculate [H⁺] in units of 10⁻³ mol/dm³.

items.text: If a mass is given, moles = mass ÷ Mr, then concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³.

items: Assume [HA] is unchanged and [H⁺] = [A⁻].
[H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]) for a weak acid.
Ka can be found from a measured pH by reversing the method.

blocks.text: The approximations work for weak acids that are very slightly dissociated. They fail for the stronger weak acids.

items: If Ka is large, a sizeable fraction of HA dissociates. Then [HA] at equilibrium is noticeably smaller than the starting concentration.
Then [HA]equilibrium ≈ [HA]undissociated is no longer valid, and the calculated [H⁺] is too high.
In very dilute solutions, H⁺ from water is no longer negligible, so [H⁺] = [A⁻] is not valid either.
A full answer needs a quadratic equation, which is not required here.
The approximations hold only for slightly dissociated acids.
For stronger weak acids the calculated [H⁺] is too high.

checks.q: Write the expression for Ka for propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.
Calculate the pH of 0.250 mol/dm³ methanoic acid, Ka = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³. State your two assumptions.
checks.a: [H⁺] = √(1.6 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.250) = 6.3 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³; pH = 2.20. Assumptions: [HA] equilibrium = [HA] initial; [H⁺] = [A⁻] (H⁺ from water negligible).

checks.q: Explain why the approximation [HA]equilibrium ≈ [HA]undissociated gives an error for a stronger weak acid.
checks.a: More of the acid dissociates, so the equilibrium [HA] is smaller than the initial concentration; the calculated [H⁺] is therefore too high.

items: Learners are not required to solve quadratic equations.
State both approximations in an answer: [HA]equilibrium ≈ [HA]undissociated, and [H⁺]equilibrium ≈ [A⁻]equilibrium.

blocks.text: Defining pKw and comparing pH data

items: **pKw** = −log₁₀Kw, which is 14.00 at 298 K.
At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid, and a strong base has a higher pH than a weak base.
A salt of a strong acid and a strong base is about pH 7. A salt of a weak acid and a strong base is above 7. A salt of a strong acid and a weak base is below 7.
Diluting a strong acid 10, 100 and 1000 times raises its pH by 1, 2 and 3.
For a weak acid [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]), so a tenfold dilution cuts [H⁺] by √10, about 3.2. The pH rises by only about 0.5 for each tenfold dilution, so about 1.5 after 1000 times.
A weak acid is also more dissociated when more dilute.
